entries.a20449f17ad5d1ebea02580f41d1f4bd720a67b2: <div sID="gen16559" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="47" osisID="Isa.47" sID="Isa.47"/> <div eID="gen16559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16560" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16561" type="x-p"/> Infinite Wisdom could have ordered things so that Israel might have been released and yet Babylon unhurt; but if they will harden their hearts, and will not let the people go, they must thank themselves that their ruin is made to pave the way to Israel's release. That ruin is here, in this chapter, largely foretold, not to gratify a spirit of revenge in the people of God, who had been used barbarously by them, but to encourage their faith and hope concerning their own deliverance, and to be a type of the downfall of that great enemy of the New-Testament church which, in the Revelation, goes under the name of "Babylon." In this chapter we have, I. The greatness of the ruin threatened, that Babylon should be brought down to the dust, and made completely miserable, should fall from the height of prosperity into the depth of adversity, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The sins that provoked God to bring this ruin upon them. 1. Their cruelty to the people of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">ver. 6</reference>. 2. Their pride and carnal security, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7-Isa.47.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. 3. Their confidence in themselves and contempt of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">ver. 10</reference>. 4. Their use of magic arts and their dependence upon enchantments and sorceries, which should be so far from standing them in any stead that they should but hasten their ruin, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.11-Isa.47.15">ver. 11-15</reference>.
entries.8c08663425e6badd48d51312e98ec6107f490c1e: <div eID="gen16561" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16560" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Babylon Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16562" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called tender and delicate. <hi type="super">2</hi> Take the millstones, and grind meal: uncover thy locks, make bare the leg, uncover the thigh, pass over the rivers. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen: I will take vengeance, and I will not meet <hi type="italic">thee as</hi> a man. <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> our redeemer, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name, the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">5</hi> Sit thou silent, and get thee into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans: for thou shalt no more be called, The lady of kingdoms. <hi type="super">6</hi> I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst show them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke. <div eID="gen16562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16563" type="x-p"/> In these verses God by the prophet sends a messenger even to Babylon, like that of Jonah to Nineveh: "The time is at hand when Babylon shall be destroyed." Fair warning is thus given her, that she may by repentance prevent the ruin and there may be a lengthening of her tranquility. We may observe here, <div eID="gen16563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16564" type="x-p"/> I. God's controversy with Babylon. We will begin with that, for there all the calamity begins; she has made God her enemy, and then who can befriend her: Let her know that the righteous Judge, to whom vengeance belongs, has said (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will take vengeance.</hi> She has provoked God, and shall be reckoned with for it when the measure of her iniquities is full. Woe to those on whom God comes to take vengeance; for who knows the power of his anger and what a fearful thing it is to fall into his hands? Were it a man like ourselves who would be revenged on us, we might hope to be a match for him, either to make our escape from him or to make our part good with him. But he says, "<hi type="italic">I will not meet thee as a man,</hi> not with the compassions of a man, but I will be to the as a lion, and a <hi type="italic">young lion</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 14</reference>); or, rather, not with the strength of a man, which is easily resisted, but with the power of a God, which cannot be resisted. Not with the justice of a man, which may be bribed, or biassed, or mollified by a foolish pity, but with the justice of a God, which is strict and severe, and can never be evaded. As in pardoning the penitent, so in punishing the impenitent, he is <hi type="italic">God and not man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">Hos. xi. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen16564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16565" type="x-p"/> II. The particular ground of this controversy. We are sure that there is cause for it, and it is a just cause; it is the <hi type="italic">vengeance of his temple</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.28">Jer. l. 28</reference>); it is for <hi type="italic">violence done to Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.35">Jer. li. 35</reference>. God will plead his people's cause against them. It is acknowledged (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">v. 6</reference>) that God had, in wrath, delivered his people into the hands of the Babylonians, had made use of them for the correction of his children, and had by their means <hi type="italic">polluted his inheritance,</hi> had left his peculiar people exposed to suffer in common with the rest of the nations, had suffered the heathen, who should have been kept at a distance, to <hi type="italic">come into his sanctuary</hi> and <hi type="italic">defile his temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.79.1">Ps. lxxix. 1</reference>. Herein God was righteous; but the Babylonians carried the matter too far, and, when they had them in their hands (triumphing to see a people that had been so much in reputation for wisdom, holiness, and honour, brought thus low), with a base and servile spirit they trampled upon them, <hi type="italic">and showed them no mercy,</hi> no, not the common instances of humanity which the miserable are entitled to purely by their misery. They used them barbarously, and with an air of contempt, nay, and of complacency in their calamities. They were brought under the yoke; but, as if that were not enough, they <hi type="italic">laid the yoke on very heavily,</hi> adding affliction to the afflicted. Nay, they laid it <hi type="italic">on the ancient</hi>—the elders in years, who were past their labour, and must sink under a yoke which those in their youthful strength would easily bear—the elders in office, those that had been judges and magistrates, and persons of the first rank. They took a pride in putting these to the meanest hardest drudgery. Jeremiah laments this, that the <hi type="italic">faces of elders were not honoured,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">Lam. v. 12</reference>. Nothing brings a surer or a sorer ruin upon any people than cruelty, especially to God's Israel. <div eID="gen16565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16566" type="x-p"/> III. The terror of this controversy. She has reason to tremble when she is told who it is that has this quarrel with her (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As for our Redeemer,</hi> our <hi type="italic">Goël,</hi> that undertakes to plead our cause as the avenger of our blood, he has two names which speak not only comfort to us, but terror to our adversaries." 1. "He is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> that has all the creatures at his command, and therefore has <hi type="italic">all power both in heaven and in earth.</hi>" Woe to those against whom the Lord fights, for the whole creation is at war with them. 2. "He is the <hi type="italic">Holy One of Israel,</hi> a God in covenant with us, who has his residence among us, and will faithfully perform all the promises he has made to us." God's power and holiness are engaged against Babylon and for Zion. This may fitly be applied to Christ, our great Redeemer. He is both Lord of hosts and the Holy One of Israel. <div eID="gen16566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16567" type="x-p"/> IV. The consequences of it to Babylon. She is called a <hi type="italic">virgin,</hi> because so she thought herself, though she was the mother of harlots. She was beautiful as a virgin, and courted by all about her; she had been called <hi type="italic">tender and delicate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">v. 1</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the lady of kingdoms</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">v. 5</reference>); but now the case is altered. 1. Her honour is gone, and she must bid farewell to all her dignity. She that had sat at the upper end of the world, sat in state and sat at ease, must now <hi type="italic">come down and sit in the dust,</hi> as very mean and a deep mourner, must <hi type="italic">sit on the ground,</hi> for she shall be so emptied and impoverished that she shall not have a seat left her to sit upon. 2. Her power is gone, and she must bid farewell to all her dominion. She shall rule no more as she has done, nor give law as she has done to her neighbours: <hi type="italic">There is no throne,</hi> none for thee, <hi type="italic">O daughter of the Chaldeans!</hi> Note, Those that abuse their honour or power provoke God to deprive them of it, and to make them <hi type="italic">come down and sit in the dust.</hi> 3. Her ease and pleasure are gone: "She shall <hi type="italic">no more be called tender and delicate</hi> as she has been, for she shall not only be deprived of all those things with which she pampered herself, but shall be put to hard service and made to feel both want and pain, which will be more than doubly grievous to her who formerly <hi type="italic">would not venture to set</hi> so much as <hi type="italic">the sole of her foot to the ground for tenderness and for delicacy,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deut. xxviii. 56</reference>. It is our wisdom not to use ourselves to be tender and delicate, because we know not how hardly others may use us before we die not what straits we may be reduced to. 4. Her liberty is gone, and she is brought into a state of servitude and as sore a bondage as she in her prosperity had brought others to. Even the great men of Babylon must now receive the same law from the conquerors that they used to give to the conquered: "<hi type="italic">Take the mill-stones and grind meal</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">v. 2</reference>), set to work, to hard labour" (like beating hemp in Bridewell), "which will make thee sweat so that thou must throw off all thy head-dresses, and <hi type="italic">uncover thy locks.</hi>" When they were driven from one place to another, at the capricious humours of their masters, they must be forced to wade up to the middle through the waters, to <hi type="italic">make bare the leg</hi> and <hi type="italic">uncover the thigh,</hi> that they might <hi type="italic">pass over the rivers,</hi> which would be a great mortification to those that used to ride in state. But let them not complain, for just thus they had formerly used their captives; and <hi type="italic">with what measure they</hi> then <hi type="italic">meted</hi> it is now <hi type="italic">measured to them again.</hi> Let those that have power use it with temper and moderation, considering that the spoke which is uppermost will be under. 5. All her glory, and all her glorying, are gone. Instead of glory, she has ignominy (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy nakedness shall be uncovered and thy shame shall be seen,</hi> according to the base and barbarous usage they commonly gave their captives, to whom, for covetousness of their clothes, they did not leave rags sufficient to cover their nakedness, so void were they of the modesty as well as of the pity due to the human nature. Instead of glorying she <hi type="italic">sits silently, and gets into darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">v. 5</reference>), ashamed to show her face, for she has quite lost her credit and <hi type="italic">shall no more be called the lady of kingdoms.</hi> Note, God can make those sit silently that used to make the greatest noise in the world, and send those into darkness that used to make the greatest figure. Let him that glories, therefore, glory in a God that changes not, and not in any worldly wealth, pleasure, or honour, which are subject to change.
entries.772b78727ce11158c807aeee689f79b75fd5f17a: <div eID="gen16567" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Babylon Threatened. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16568" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And thou saidst, I shall be a lady for ever: <hi type="italic">so</hi> that thou didst not lay these <hi type="italic">things</hi> to thy heart, neither didst remember the latter end of it. <hi type="super">8</hi> Therefore hear now this, <hi type="italic">thou that art</hi> given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I <hi type="italic">am,</hi> and none else beside me; I shall not sit <hi type="italic">as</hi> a widow, neither shall I know the loss of children: <hi type="super">9</hi> But these two <hi type="italic">things</hi> shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, <hi type="italic">and</hi> for the great abundance of thine enchantments. <hi type="super">10</hi> For thou hast trusted in thy wickedness: thou hast said, None seeth me. Thy wisdom and thy knowledge, it hath perverted thee; and thou hast said in thine heart, I <hi type="italic">am,</hi> and none else beside me. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore shall evil come upon thee; thou shalt not know from whence it riseth: and mischief shall fall upon thee; thou shalt not be able to put it off: and desolation shall come upon thee suddenly, <hi type="italic">which</hi> thou shalt not know. <hi type="super">12</hi> Stand now with thine enchantments, and with the multitude of thy sorceries, wherein thou hast laboured from thy youth; if so be thou shalt be able to profit, if so be thou mayest prevail. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels. Let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up, and save thee from <hi type="italic">these things</hi> that shall come upon thee. <hi type="super">14</hi> Behold, they shall be as stubble; the fire shall burn them; they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame: <hi type="italic">there shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> a coal to warm at, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> fire to sit before it. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thus shall they be unto thee with whom thou hast laboured, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thy merchants, from thy youth: they shall wander every one to his quarter; none shall save thee. <div eID="gen16568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16569" type="x-p"/> Babylon, now doomed to ruin, is here justly upbraided with her pride, luxury, and security, in the day of her prosperity, and the confidence she had in her own wisdom and forecast, and particularly in the prognostications and counsels of the astrologers. These things are mentioned both to justify God in bringing these judgments upon her and to mortify her, and put her to so much the greater shame, under these judgments; for, when God comes forth to take vengeance, glory belongs to him, but confusion to the sinner. <div eID="gen16569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16570" type="x-p"/> I. The Babylonians are here upbraided with their pride and haughtiness, and the great conceit they had of themselves, because of their wealth and power, and the vast extent of their dominion; it was the language both of the government and of the body of the people: <hi type="italic">Thou sayest in thy heart</hi> (and God, who searches all hearts, can tell men what they say there, though they never speak it out) <hi type="italic">I am, and none else besides me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">10</reference>. The repetition of this part of the charge intimates that they said it often, and that it was very offensive to God. It is the very word that God has often said concerning himself, <hi type="italic">I am, and none else besides me,</hi> denoting his self-existence, his infinite and incomparable perfections, and his sole supremacy. All this Babylon pretends to; and no wonder if she that assumed a power to make what gods and goddesses she pleased for the people to worship made herself one among the rest. It is presumption to say of any creature, "It is, and there is not its like, there is none besides it" (for creatures stand very nearly upon a level with one another); but it is insufferable arrogance for any to say so of themselves, and an evidence of their self-ignorance. <div eID="gen16570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16571" type="x-p"/> II. They are upbraided with their luxury and love of ease (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou that art given to pleasures,</hi> art a slave to them, art in them as in thy element, and, that thou mayest enjoy them without disturbance or interruption, <hi type="italic">dwellest carelessly</hi> and layest nothing to heart." Great wealth and plenty are great temptations to sensuality, and, where there is fulness of bread, there is commonly abundance of idleness. But if those that are given to pleasures, and dwell carelessly, would but hear this, that <hi type="italic">for all these things God will bring them into judgment,</hi> it would be a damp to their mirth, an allay to their pleasure, and would find them something to be in care about. <div eID="gen16571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16572" type="x-p"/> III. They are upbraided with their carnal security and their vain confidence of the perpetuity of their pomps and pleasures. This is much insisted on here. Observe, <div eID="gen16572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16573" type="x-p"/> 1. The cause of their security. They thought themselves safe and out of danger, not because they were ignorant of the uncertainty of all earthly enjoyments and the inevitable fate that attends states and kingdoms as well as particular persons, but <hi type="italic">because they did not lay this to heart,</hi> did not apply it to themselves, nor give it a due consideration. They lulled themselves asleep in ease and pleasure, and dreamt of nothing else but that <hi type="italic">to-morrow should be as this day, and much more abundant.</hi> They did not <hi type="italic">remember the latter end of it</hi>—the latter end of their prosperity, that it is a fading flower, and will wither—the latter end of their iniquity, that it will be bitterness, that the day will come when their injustice and oppression must be reckoned for and punished. <hi type="italic">She did not remember her latter end</hi> (so some read it); she forgot that her day would come to fall and what would be in the end hereof. It was the ruin of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.9">Lam. i. 9</reference>) that <hi type="italic">she remembered not her last end, therefore she came down wonderfully;</hi> and it was Babylon's ruin too. The children of men are easy, and think themselves safe, in their sinful ways, only because they never think of death, and judgment, and their future state. <div eID="gen16573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16574" type="x-p"/> 2. The ground of their security. They trusted in their wickedness and in their wisdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">v. 10</reference>. (1.) Their power and wealth, which they had gotten by fraud and oppression, were their confidence: <hi type="italic">Thou hast trusted in thy wickedness,</hi> As Doeg. <reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 7</reference>. Many have so debauched their own consciences, and have got to such a pitch of daring wickedness, that they stick at nothing; and this they trust to carry them through those difficulties which embarrass men who make conscience of what they say and do. They doubt not but they shall be too hard for all their enemies, because they dare lie, and kill, and forswear themselves, and do any thing for their interest. Thus they trust in their wickedness to secure them, which is the only thing that will ruin them. (2.) Their policy and craft, which they called their <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> were their confidence. They thought they could outwit all mankind, and therefore might set all their enemies at defiance. But their <hi type="italic">wisdom and knowledge perverted them,</hi> and turned them out of the way, made them forget themselves, and the preparation necessary to be made for hereafter. <div eID="gen16574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16575" type="x-p"/> 3. The expressions of their security. Three things this proud and haughty monarchy said, in her security:— (1.) "<hi type="italic">I shall be a lady for ever,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7">v. 7</reference>. She looked upon the patent of her honour to be not merely during the pleasure of the sovereign Lord, the fountain of honour, or during her own good behaviour, but to be perpetual to the present generation and their heirs and successors for ever. She was not only proud that she was a lady, but confident that she should be a lady for ever. Thus the New-Testament Babylon says, <hi type="italic">I sit as a queen, and shall see no sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Rev. xviii. 7</reference>. Those ladies mistake themselves, and consider not their latter end, who think they shall be ladies for ever; for death will shortly lay their honour with them in the dust. Saints will be saints for ever, but lords and ladies will not be so for ever. (2.) "<hi type="italic">I shall not sit as a widow,</hi> in solitude and sorrow, shall never lose the power and wealth I am thus wedded to; the monarchy shall never want a monarch to espouse and protect it, and be a husband to the state; <hi type="italic">nor shall I know the loss of children,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">v. 8</reference>. She was as confident of the continuance of the numbers of her people as of the dignity of her prince, and had no fear of being either deposed or depopulated. Those that are in the height of prosperity are apt to fancy themselves out of the reach of adverse fate. (3.) "<hi type="italic">No one sees me</hi> when I do amiss, and therefore there will be none to call me to an account," <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">v. 10</reference>. It is common for sinners to promise themselves impunity, because they promise themselves secrecy, in their wicked ways. They trust to their wicked arts and designs to stand them in stead, because they think they have carried them on so plausibly that none can discern the wickedness and deceit of them. <div eID="gen16575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16576" type="x-p"/> 4. The punishment of their security. It shall be their ruin; and it will be, (1.) A complete ruin, the ruin of all their comforts and confidences: "<hi type="italic">These two things shall come upon thee</hi> (the very two things that thou didst set at defiance), <hi type="italic">loss of children and widowhood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.9">v. 9</reference>. Both thy princes and thy people shall be cut off, so that thou shalt be no more a government, no more a nation." Note, God often brings upon secure sinners those very mischiefs which they least feared and thought themselves in least danger of. "<hi type="italic">They shall come upon thee in their perfection,</hi> with all their aggravating circumstances and without any thing to allay or mitigate them." Afflictions to God's children are not afflictions in perfection. Widowhood is not to them a calamity in perfection, for they have this to comfort themselves with, that their Maker is their husband; loss of children is not, for he is better to them than ten sons. But on his enemies they come in perfection. Widowhood and loss of children are either of them great griefs, but both together great indeed. Naomi thinks she may well be called <hi type="italic">Marah</hi> when she is <hi type="italic">left both of her sons and of her husband</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.1.5">Ruth i. 5</reference>); and yet on her these evils did not come in perfection, for she had two daughters-in-law left, that were comforts to her. But on Babylon they come in perfection; she has no comfort remaining. (2.) It will be a sudden and surprising ruin. The evil shall come <hi type="italic">in one day,</hi> nay, <hi type="italic">in a moment,</hi> which will make it much the more terrible, especially to those that were so very secure. "<hi type="italic">Evil shall come upon thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.11">v. 11</reference>) and thou shalt have neither time nor way to provide against it, or to prepare for it; for <hi type="italic">thou shalt not know whence it rises,</hi> and therefore shalt not know where to stand upon thy guard." <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not know the morning thereof;</hi> so the Hebrew phrase is. We know just when and where the day will break and the sun rise, but we know not what the day, when it comes, will bring forth, nor when or where trouble will arise; perhaps the storm may come from that point of the compass which we little thought of. Babylon pretended to great wisdom and knowledge (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">v. 10</reference>), but with all her knowledge she cannot foresee, nor with all her wisdom prevent, the ruin threatened: "<hi type="italic">Desolation shall come upon thee suddenly,</hi> as a thief in the night, <hi type="italic">which thou shalt not know,</hi> that is, which thou little thoughtest of." Fair warning was indeed given them, by Isaiah and other prophets of the Lord, of this desolation; but they slighted that notice, and would give no credit to it, and therefore justly is it so ordered that they should have no other notice of it, but that partly through their own security, and partly through the swiftness and subtlety of the enemy, when it came it should be a perfect surprise to them. Those that slight the warnings of the written word, let them not expect any other premonitions. (3.) It will be an irresistible ruin, and such as they will have no fence against: "<hi type="italic">Mischief shall come upon thee</hi> so suddenly that thou shalt have no time to turn thee in, so strongly that thou shalt not be able to make head against it and to put it off and save thyself." There is no opposing the judgments of God when they come with commission. Babylon herself, with all her wealth, and power, and multitude, is not able to put off the mischief that comes. <div eID="gen16576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16577" type="x-p"/> IV. They are upbraided with their divinations, their magical and astrological arts and sciences, which the Chaldeans, above any other nation, were notorious for, and from them other nations borrowed all their learning of that kind. <div eID="gen16577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16578" type="x-p"/> 1. This is here spoken of as one of their provoking sins, which would bring the judgments of God upon them, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.9">v. 9</reference>. "These evils shall come upon thee to punish thee <hi type="italic">for the multitude of thy sorceries, and the great abundance of thy enchantments.</hi>" Witchcraft is a sin in its own nature exceedingly heinous; it is giving that honour to the devil which is due to God only, making God's enemy our guide and the father of lies our oracle. In Babylon it was a national sin, and had the protection and countenance of the government; conjurors, for aught that appears, were their privy counsellors and prime ministers of state. And shall not God visit for these things? Observe what a multitude, what a great abundance, of sorceries and enchantments there were among them. Such a bewitching sin this was that when it was once admitted it spread like wildfire, and they never knew any end of it; the deceived and the deceivers both increased strangely. <div eID="gen16578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16579" type="x-p"/> 2. It is here spoken of as one of their vain confidences, which they relied much upon, but should be deceived in, for it would not serve so much as to give them notice of the judgments coming, much less to guard against them. (1.) They are here upbraided with the mighty pains they had taken about their sorceries and enchantments: Thou hast <hi type="italic">laboured in them from thy youth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12">v. 12</reference>. They trained up their young men in these studies, and those that applied themselves to them were indefatigable in their labours about them—reading books, making observations, trying experiments. Well, let them stand up now with their enchantments, and try their skill in the critical moment. Let them make a stand, if they can, in opposition to the invading enemy; let them stand to offer their service to their country; but to what purpose? "<hi type="italic">Thou art wearied in the multitude of thy counsels</hi> of this kind (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">v. 13</reference>); thou hast advised with them all, but hast received no satisfaction from them; the different schemes they have erected, and the different judgments they have given, have but increased thy perplexity and tired thee out." In the multitude of such counsellors there is no safety. (2.) They are upbraided with the variety they had of such kinds of people among them, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">v. 13</reference>. They had their <hi type="italic">astrologers,</hi> or viewers of the heavens, that did not consider them, as David, to behold the wisdom and power of God in them; but, under pretence of foretelling future events by them, they viewed the heavens and forgot him that made them and set <hi type="italic">their dominion on the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.33">Job xxxviii. 33</reference>), and has himself dominion over them, for he rides on the heavens. They had their <hi type="italic">star-gazers,</hi> who by the motions of the stars, their conjunctions and oppositions, read the doom of states and kingdoms. They had their <hi type="italic">monthly prognosticators,</hi> their almanac-makers, that told what weather it should be or what news they should have each month. The great stock they had of these was what they valued themselves much upon; but they were all cheats, and their art was a sham. I confess I see not how the judicial astrology which some now pretend to, by the rules of which they undertake to prophecy concerning things to come, can be distinguished from that of the Chaldeans, nor therefore how it can escape the censure and contempt which this text lays that under; yet I fear there are some who study their almanacs, and regard them and their prognostications, more than their Bibles and the prophecies there. (3.) They are upbraided with the utter inability and insufficiency of all these pretenders to do them any kindness in the day of their distress. Let them see whether with the help of their enchantments they can prevail against their enemies, or profit themselves, inspirit their own forces or dispirit those that come against them, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12">v. 12</reference>. Let them see what service those can do them who make a trade of divination: "<hi type="italic">Let them stand up,</hi> and either by their power save thee from these evils that are coming upon thee or by their foresight make such a discovery of them beforehand that thou mayest by needful precautions save thyself;" as Elisha, by notifying to the king of Israel the motions of the Syrian army, enabled him to <hi type="italic">save himself, not once nor twice,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.10">2 Kings vi. 10</reference>. This baffling of the diviners was literally fulfilled when, the night that Babylon was taken and Belshazzar slain, all his astrologers, soothsayers, and wise men, were quite nonplussed with the handwriting on the wall that pronounced the fatal sentence, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.8">Dan. v. 8</reference>. (4.) They are upbraided with the fall of the wise men themselves in the common ruin, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.14">v. 14</reference>. Those are unlikely to stand their friends in any stead who cannot secure themselves; they are as stubble at the best, worthless and useless, and <hi type="italic">they shall be as stubble</hi> before a consuming fire. The Persians, to make room for their own wise men, will cut off those of Babylon; that <hi type="italic">fire shall burn them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">they shall not deliver themselves from the power of the flame.</hi> Those can expect no other than to be devoured by their sins make themselves fuel to a devouring fire. When God kindles a fire among them it <hi type="italic">shall not be a coal to warm at,</hi> and <hi type="italic">a fire to sit before,</hi> but a coal to burn them. Or, rather, it denotes that they shall be utterly consumed by the judgments of God, burnt quite to ashes, and there shall not remain one live coal to do any body any service; for <hi type="italic">when God judges he will overcome.</hi> (5.) They are upbraided with their merchants, and those they dealt with (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.15">v. 15</reference>), such as they dealt with from their youth, either, [1.] In a way of consultation. These astrologers, that dealt in the black art, they always loved to be dealing with, and they were in effect their merchants; fortune-telling was one of the best trades in Babylon, and those that followed that trade probably lived as splendidly and got as much money as the richest merchants; yet, when some of them were devoured, others fled their country, <hi type="italic">every one to his quarter,</hi> and there was none to save Babylon. Miserable comforters are they all. Or, [2.] In a way of commerce. As their astrologers, with whom they had laboured, failed them, so did their merchants; they took care to secure their own effects, and then valued not what became of Babylon. They <hi type="italic">wandered every one to his own quarter;</hi> each man shifted for his own safety, but none would offer to lend a helping hand, no, not to a city by which they had got so much money. Every one was for himself, but few for his friends. The New-Testament Babylon is lamented by the merchants that were made rich by her, but they very prudently stand afar off to lament her (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.15">Rev. xviii. 15</reference>), not willing to attempt any thing for her succour. Happy are those who by faith and prayer deal with one that will be a <hi type="italic">very present help in time of trouble!</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.47"/> <div eID="gen16579" type="x-p"/>

entries.fcc4bed452e91d276006e5ce8c3cfb9b507d04df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9226"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 47</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.15">Is 47:1-15</reference>. The Destruction of Babylon Is Represented under the Image of a Royal Virgin Brought Down in a Moment from Her Magnificent Throne to the Extreme of Degradation.</title> <div sID="gen15741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9226"/><hi type="bold">1. in the dust--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.3.26">Is 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">La 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen15741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgin--</hi>that is, heretofore uncaptured [Herodotus, 1.191].<div eID="gen15742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughter of Babylon--</hi>Babylon and its inhabitants (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Is 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Is 37:22</reference>).<div eID="gen15743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no throne--</hi>The seat of empire was transferred to Shushan. Alexander intended to have made Babylon his seat of empire, but Providence defeated his design. He soon died; and Seleucia, being built near, robbed it of its inhabitants, and even of its name, which was applied to Seleucia.<div eID="gen15744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delicate--</hi>alluding to the effeminate debauchery and prostitution of all classes at banquets and religious rites [Curtius, 5.1; Herodotus, 1.199; Baruch, 6.43]. <div eID="gen15745" type="x-p"/>
entries.facbbdcedcb19822b75b44376568812a2aec4630: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9227"/><div sID="gen15746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9227"/><hi type="bold">2. millstones--</hi>like the querns or hand-mills, found in this country, before the invention of water mills and windmills: a convex stone, made by the hand to turn in a concave stone, fitted to receive it, the corn being ground between them: the office of a female slave in the East; most degrading (<reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.41">Mt 24:41</reference>).<div eID="gen15746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncover thy locks--</hi>rather, "take off thy veil" [Horsley]: perhaps the removal of the plaited hair worn round the women's temples is included; it, too, is a covering (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.15">1Co 11:15</reference>); to remove it and the veil is the badge of the lowest female degradation; in the East the head is the seat of female modesty; the face of a woman is seldom, the whole head almost never, seen bare (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8">Is 22:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make bare the leg--</hi>rather "lift up (literally, 'uncover'; as in lifting up the train the leg is uncovered) thy flowing train." In Mesopotamia, women of low rank, as occasion requires, wade across the rivers with stript legs, or else entirely put off their garments and swim across. "Exchange thy rich, loose, queenly robe, for the most abject condition, that of one going to and fro through rivers as a slave, to draw water," &c.<div eID="gen15748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncover ... thigh--</hi>gather up the robe, so as to wade across. <div eID="gen15749" type="x-p"/>
entries.07f46733dd8d835d9b5160b1112b2cba960abbd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9228"/><div sID="gen15750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9228"/><hi type="bold">3. not meet ... as a man--</hi>rather, "I will not meet a man," that is, suffer man to intercede with me--give man an audience [Horsley]. Or, "I will not make peace with any man," before all are destroyed. Literally, "strike a league with"; a phrase arising from the custom of striking hands together in making a compact [Maurer], (see on <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">Pr 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.26">Pr 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">11:15</reference>, Margin). Or else from striking the victims sacrificed in making treaties. <div eID="gen15750" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ad11464e3f3298de0bb41325a535eb758a94bbf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9229"/><div sID="gen15751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9229"/><hi type="bold">4. As for--</hi>rather supply, "Thus saith our Redeemer" [Maurer]. Lowth supposes this verse to be the exclamation of a chorus breaking in with praises, "Our Redeemer! Jehovah of hosts," &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.34">Jr 50:34</reference>). <div eID="gen15751" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb70a0b79764a46ca0b8402772da18b04b02d55c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9230"/><div sID="gen15752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9230"/><hi type="bold">5. Sit--</hi>the posture of mourning (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.4">Ezr 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">La 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen15752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>mourning and misery (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.2">La 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">Mi 7:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lady of kingdoms--</hi>mistress of the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Is 13:19</reference>). <div eID="gen15754" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea53b9e0ef3b18a3601f13ea0eb2c4a1001d6eb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9231"/><div sID="gen15755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9231"/>6. reason for God's vengeance on Babylon: in executing God's will against His people, she had done so with wanton cruelty (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">Jr 50:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">51:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zec 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen15755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">polluted my inheritance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.43.28">Is 43:28</reference>).<div eID="gen15756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the ancient--</hi>Even old age was disregarded by the Chaldeans, who treated all alike with cruelty (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">La 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">5:12</reference>) [Rosenmuller]. Or, "the ancient" means Israel, worn out with calamities in the latter period of its history (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Is 46:4</reference>), as its earlier stage of history is called its "youth" (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.6">Is 54:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60">Eze 16:60</reference>). <div eID="gen15757" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c6a2a4a9433ac198e959294c2109c3104c257d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9232"/><div sID="gen15758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9232"/><hi type="bold">7. so that--</hi>Through thy vain expectation of being a queen for ever, thou didst advance to such a pitch of insolence as not to believe "these things" (namely, as to thy overthrow, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.5">Is 47:1-5</reference>) possible.<div eID="gen15758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">end of it--</hi>namely, of thy insolence, implied in her words, "I shall be a lady for ever." <div eID="gen15759" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ce2c7dd4dc696c6675be8e999fcd58c281aa0ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9233"/><div sID="gen15760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9233"/><hi type="bold">8. given to pleasures--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">Is 47:1</reference>). In no city were there so many incentives to licentiousness.<div eID="gen15760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am ... none ... beside me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">Is 47:10</reference>). Language of arrogance in man's mouth; fitting for God alone (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.6">Is 45:6</reference>). See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Is 5:8</reference>, latter part.<div eID="gen15761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">widow ... loss of children--</hi>A state, represented as a female, when it has fallen is called a widow, because its king is no more; and childless, because it has no inhabitants; they having been carried off as captives (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.4">Is 23:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">54:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Re 18:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen15762" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c0472282dcb446a7add23d10d418acb2d64e223: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9234"/><div sID="gen15763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9234"/><hi type="bold">9. in a moment--</hi>It should not decay slowly, but be suddenly and unexpectedly destroyed; in a single night it was taken by Cyrus. The prophecy was again literally fulfilled when Babylon revolted against Darius; and, in order to hold out to the last, each man chose one woman of his family, and strangled the rest, to save provisions. Darius impaled three thousand of the revolters.<div eID="gen15763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... perfection--</hi>that is, "in full measure."<div eID="gen15764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ... for--</hi>rather, "notwithstanding the ... notwithstanding"; "in spite of" [Lowth]. So "for" (<reference osisRef="Num.14.11">Nu 14:11</reference>). Babylon was famous for "expiations or sacrifices, and other incantations, whereby they tried to avert evil and obtain good" [Diodorus Siculus]. <div eID="gen15765" type="x-p"/>
entries.1b3a1f1269f43ec9710ee1d9a4ff7ab88c4f6641: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9235"/><div sID="gen15766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9235"/><hi type="bold">10. wickedness--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Is 13:11</reference>, the cruelty with which Babylon treated its subject states.<div eID="gen15766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">None seeth me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">94:7</reference>). "There is none to exact punishment from me." Sinners are not safe, though seeming secret.<div eID="gen15767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thy wisdom--</hi>astrological and political (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">Is 19:11</reference>, &c., as to Egypt).<div eID="gen15768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perverted--</hi>turns thee aside from the right and safe path. <div eID="gen15769" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe2761097c1fca568d32ca0bbf3a3280c8ba18ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9236"/><div sID="gen15770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9236"/><hi type="bold">11. from whence it riseth--</hi>Hebrew, "the dawn thereof," that is, its first rising. Evil shall come on thee without the least previous intimation [Rosenmuller]. But dawn is not applied to "evil," but to prosperity shining out after misery (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Is 21:12</reference>). Translate, "Thou shall not see any dawn" (of alleviation) [Maurer].<div eID="gen15770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put ... off--</hi>rather, as Margin, "remove by expiation"; it shall be never ending.<div eID="gen15771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not know--</hi>unawares: which thou dost not apprehend. Proving the fallacy of thy divinations and astrology (<reference osisRef="Job.9.5">Job 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.8">Psa 35:8</reference>). <div eID="gen15772" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bb76293f8455071158c6cca4c3ce2bcbe322ad8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9237"/><div sID="gen15773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9237"/><hi type="bold">12. Stand--</hi>forth: a scornful challenge to Babylon's magicians to show whether they can defend their city.<div eID="gen15773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laboured--</hi>The devil's service is a laborious yet fruitless one (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Is 55:2</reference>). <div eID="gen15774" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fa7d92a607e5b51ede13d5948b51b447ff26b1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9238"/><div sID="gen15775" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9238"/><hi type="bold">13. wearied--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Isa.57.10">Is 57:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.12">Eze 24:12</reference>).<div eID="gen15775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">astrologers--</hi>literally, those who form combinations of the heavens; who watch conjunctions and oppositions of the stars. "Casters of the configurations of the sky" [Horsley]. Gesenius explains it: the dividers of the heavens. In casting a nativity they observed four signs:--the horoscope, or sign which arose at the time one was born; the mid-heaven; the sign opposite the horoscope towards the west; and the hypogee.<div eID="gen15776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">monthly prognosticators--</hi>those who at each new moon profess to tell thereby what is about to happen. Join, not as English Version, "save ... from those things," &c.; but, "They that at new moons make known from (by means of) them the things that shall come upon thee" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen15777" type="x-p"/>
entries.c494a158ad1ba3c604b03451cb1837dc5d2f97ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9239"/><div sID="gen15778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9239"/>14. (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">30:30</reference>).<div eID="gen15778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... a coal--</hi>Like stubble, they shall burn to a dead ash, without leaving a live coal or cinder (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.30.14">Is 30:14</reference>), so utterly shall they be destroyed. <div eID="gen15779" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddb5efc0428cdb718b5f184216690489c8b0d94a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9240"/><div sID="gen15780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9240"/><hi type="bold">15. Thus, &c.--</hi>Such shall be the fate of those astrologers who cost thee such an amount of trouble and money.<div eID="gen15780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy merchants, from thy youth--</hi>that is, with whom thou hast trafficked from thy earliest history, the foreigners sojourning in Babylon for the sake of commerce (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.14">Is 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">Jr 51:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.16">Na 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.17">17</reference>) [Barnes]. Rather, the astrologers, with whom Babylon had so many dealings (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.12-Isa.47.14">Is 47:12-14</reference>) [Horsley].<div eID="gen15781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15782" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to his quarter--</hi>literally, "straight before him" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.9">Eze 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>). The foreigners, whether soothsayers or merchants, shall flee home out of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.16">Jr 50:16</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.47"/>

entries.2011300f35a7975aecc4753f340a262e383dcc2a: <div eID="gen28400" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28401" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28402" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28402" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28401" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28403" type="x-p"/> The destruction of Babylon is denounced by a beautiful selection of circumstances, in which her prosperous is contrasted with her adverse condition. She is represented as a tender and delicate female reduced to the work and abject condition of a slave, and bereaved of every consolation, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.4">Isa 47:1-4</reference>. And that on account of her cruelty, particularly to God's people, her pride, voluptuousness, sorceries, and incantations, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.5-Isa.47.11">Isa 47:5-11</reference>. The folly of these last practices elegantly exposed by the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12-Isa.47.15">Isa 47:12-15</reference>. It is worthy of observation that almost all the imagery of this chapter is applied in the book of the Revelation, (in nearly the same words), to the antitype of the illustrious capital of the Chaldean empire, viz., Babylon the Great. <div eID="gen28403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28404" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28405" type="x-p"/> Come down, and set in the dust "Descend, and sit on the dust" - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.3.26">Isa 3:26</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Isa.52.2">Isa 52:2</reference> (note).
entries.0c1780a205e57150802ba2d6b3d006cf2f5a7e9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28406" type="x-p"/> Take the millstones, and grind meal "Take the mill, and grind corn" - It was the work of slaves to grind the corn. They used hand-mills: water-mills were not invented till a little before the time of Augustus, (see the Greek epigram of Antipater, which seems to celebrate it as a new invention, Anthol. Cephalae, 653); wind-mills, not until long after. It was not only the work of slaves, but the hardest work; and often inflicted upon them as a severe punishment: - <div eID="gen28406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28407" type="x-p"/> Molendum in pistrino; vapulandum; habendae compedes. <div eID="gen28407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28408" type="x-p"/> Terent. Phorm. 2:1. 19. <div eID="gen28408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28409" type="x-p"/> Hominem pistrino dignum. <div eID="gen28409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28410" type="x-p"/> Id. Heaut. 3:2. 19. <div eID="gen28410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28411" type="x-p"/> To grind in the mill, to be scourged, to be put in the stocks, were punishments for slaves. Hence a delinquent was said to be a man worthy of the mill. The tread-mill, now in use in England, is a revival of this ancient usage. But in the east grinding was the work of the female slaves. See <reference osisRef="Exo.11.5">Exo 11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.12.29">Exo 12:29</reference>, (in the version of the Septuagint;) <reference osisRef="Mat.24.41">Mat 24:41</reference>; Homer, Odyss. 20:105-108. And it is the same to this day. "Women alone are employed to grind their corn;" Shaw's Algiers and Tunis, p. 287. "They are the female slaves, that are generally employed in the east at those hand-mills for grinding corn; it is extremely laborious, and esteemed the lowest employment in the house;" Sir J. Chardin, Harmer's Observ. i., p. 153. The words denote that state of captivity to which the Babylonians should be reduced. <div eID="gen28411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28412" type="x-p"/> Make bare the leg, uncover the thigh - This is repeatedly seen in Bengal, where there are few bridges, and both sexes, having neither shoes nor stockings, truss up their loose garments, and walk across, where the waters are not deep. In the deeper water they are obliged to truss very high, to which there seems a reference in the third verse: Thy nakedness shall be uncovered.
entries.ca5854fe578cad9e7761183ecc1318ed4e4e7f9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen28412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28413" type="x-p"/> I will not meet thee as a man "Neither will I suffer man to intercede with me" - The verb should be pointed, or written, אפגיע aphgia, in Hiphil.
entries.1a174d705dd5de26589adcb625272781e84d718f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen28413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28414" type="x-p"/> Our Redeemer "Our Avenger" - Here a chorus breaks in upon the midst of the subject, with a change of construction, as well as sentiment, from the longer to the shorter kind of verse, for one distich only; after which the former subject and style are resumed. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Isa 45:16</reference> (note).
entries.e824d6ca49f1ed8c92e58c1c4393818bf420c7e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28415" type="x-p"/> I was wroth with my people - God, in the course of his providence, makes use of great conquerors and tyrants as his instruments to execute his judgments in the earth; he employs one wicked nation to scourge another. The inflicter of the punishment may perhaps be as culpable as the sufferer; and may add to his guilt by indulging his cruelty in executing God's justice. When he has fulfilled the work to which the Divine vengeance has ordained him, he will become himself the object of it; see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5-Isa.10.12">Isa 10:5-12</reference>. God charges the Babylonians, though employed by himself to chastise his people, with cruelty in regard to them. They exceeded the bounds of justice and humanity in oppressing and destroying them; and though they were really executing the righteous decree of God, yet, as far as it regarded themselves, they were only indulging their own ambition and violence. The Prophet Zechariah sets this matter in the same light: "I was but a little angry and they helped forward the affliction;" <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Isa 1:15</reference>. - L.
entries.90b451eb0bf5aea4a3399147307b002b3c117a9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28416" type="x-p"/> So that thou didst not "Because thou didst not" - For עד ad, read על al; so two MSS., and one edition. And for, אחריתה acharithah, "the latter end of it, "read אחריתך acharithecha, "thy latter end;" so thirteen MSS., and two editions, and the Vulgate. Both the sixth and seventh verses are wanting in one of my oldest MSS.
entries.b58e9cc9f6268bc36466dd801cce618b4ec54c10: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28417" type="x-p"/> These two things shall come to thee in a moment - That is, suddenly. Belshazzar was slain; thus the city became metaphorically a widow, the husband - the governor of it, being slain. In the time in which the king was slain, the Medes and Persians took the city, and slew many of its inhabitants, see <reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Dan 5:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.31">Dan 5:31</reference>. When Darius took the city, he is said to have crucified three thousand of its principal inhabitants. <div eID="gen28417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28418" type="x-p"/> In their perfection "On a sudden" - Instead of בתמם bethummam, "in their perfection," as our translation renders it, the Septuagint and Syriac read, in the copies from which they translated, פתאם pithom, suddenly; parallel to רגע rega, in a moment, in the preceding alternate member of the sentence. The concurrent testimony of the Septuagint and Syriac, favored by the context, may be safely opposed to the authority of the present text. <div eID="gen28418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28419" type="x-p"/> For the multitude "Notwithstanding the multitude" - ברב berob. For this sense of the particle ב beth, see <reference osisRef="Num.14.11">Num 14:11</reference>.
entries.76fae4a16965fbd8ae105bc6c3bc1b3fd42e7fc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28420" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not know from whence it riseth "Thou shalt not know how to deprecate" - שחרה shachrah; so the Chaldee renders it, which is approved by Jarchi on the place; and Michaelis Epim. in Praelect. xix.; see <reference osisRef="Psa.78.34">Psa 78:34</reference>. <div eID="gen28420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28421" type="x-p"/> Videtur in fine hujus commatis deese verbum, ut hoc membrum prioribus respondeat. "A word appears to be wanting at the end of this clause to connect it properly with the two preceding." - Secker. <div eID="gen28421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28422" type="x-p"/> In order to set in a proper light this judicious remark, it is necessary to give the reader an exact verbal translation of the whole verse: - "And evil shall come upon thee, thou shalt not know how to deprecate it; <div eID="gen28422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28423" type="x-p"/> And mischief shall fall upon thee, thou shalt not be able to expiate it; <div eID="gen28423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28424" type="x-p"/> And destruction shall come suddenly upon thee, thou shalt not know" - <div eID="gen28424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28425" type="x-p"/> What? how to escape, to avoid it, to be delivered from it? perhaps צאת ממנה tseth mimmennah, "they could not go out from it, "<reference osisRef="Jer.11.11">Jer 11:11</reference>. I am persuaded that a phrase is here lost out of the text. But as the ancient versions retain no traces of it, and a wide field lies open to uncertain conjecture, I have not attempted to fill up the chasm, but have in the translation, as others have done before me, palliated and disguised the defect, which I cannot with any assurance pretend to supply. - L.
entries.001f62773c889beb0ad74ebfd6761453911fe57c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28426" type="x-p"/> From these things "What are the events" - For מאשר measher, read מה אשר mah asher, so the Septuagint, "what is to happen to thee."
entries.23fa17c26be5628a121f07f21bf19893e6c2ab2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen28426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28427" type="x-p"/> To his quarter "To his own business" - לעברו leebro. Expositors give no very good account of this word in this place. In a MS. it was at first לעבדו leabdo, to his servant or work, which is probably the true reading. The sense however is pretty much the same with the common interpretation: "Every one shall turn aside to his own business; none shall deliver thee."  <chapter eID="Isa.47"/> <div eID="gen28427" type="x-p"/>

entries.dc4de09be2e287ac26a7f850ed65069367014e74: <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.4">Isa 47:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen13441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13442" type="x-p"/> From the gods of Babylon the proclamation of judgment passes onto Babylon itself. <hi type="italic">“Come down, and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter Babel; sit on the ground without a throne, O Chaldaeans-daughter! For men no longer call thee delicate and voluptuous. Take the mill, and grind meal: throw back they veil, lift up the train, uncover the thigh, wade through streams. Let thy nakedness be uncovered, even let thy shame be seen; I shall take vengeance, and not spare men. Our Redeemer, Jehovah of hosts is His name, Holy One of Israel.”</hi> This is the first strophe in the prophecy. As v. 36 clearly shows, what precedes is a penal sentence from Jehovah. Both בּת in relation to בּתוּלת (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.12">Isa 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa 37:22</reference>), and בּבל and כּשׂדּים in relation to בּת, are appositional genitives; Babel and Chaldeans (כשׂדים as in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">Isa 48:20</reference>) are regarded as a woman, and that as one not yet dishonoured. The unconquered oppressor is threatened with degradation from her proud eminence into shameful humiliation; sitting on the ground is used in the same sense as in Isa 3:26. Hitherto men have called her, with envious admiration, <hi type="italic">rakkâh</hi> <hi type="italic">va‛ânuggâh</hi> (from <reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deu 28:56</reference>), <hi type="italic">mollis et delicata</hi>, as having carefully kept everything disagreeable at a distance, and revelled in nothing but luxury (compare <hi type="italic">‛ōneg</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.22">Isa 13:22</reference>). Debauchery with its attendant rioting (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Isa 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.5">Isa 25:5</reference>), and the Mylitta worship with its licensed prostitution (Herod. i. 199), were current there; but now all this was at an end. תוסיפי, according to the Masora, has only one <hi type="italic">pashta</hi> both here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">Isa 47:5</reference>, and so has the tone upon the last syllable, and accordingly <hi type="italic">metheg</hi> in the <hi type="italic">antepenult</hi>. Isaiah’s artistic style may be readily perceived both in the three clauses of <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">Isa 47:1</reference> that are comparable to a long trumpet-blast (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.40.9">Isa 40:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa 16:1</reference>), and also in the short, rugged, involuntarily excited clauses that follow. The mistress becomes the maid, and has to perform the low, menial service of those who, as Homer says in <hi type="italic">Od.</hi> vii. 104, ἀλετρεύουσι μύλης ἔπι μήλοπα καρπόν (grind at the mill the quince-coloured fruit; compare at <reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference>). She has to leave her palace as a prisoner of war, and, laying aside all feminine modesty, to wade through the rivers upon which she borders. <hi type="italic">Chespı̄</hi> has <hi type="italic">ĕ</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ĭ</hi>, and, as in other cases where a sibilant precedes, the mute <hi type="italic">p</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">f</hi> (compare <hi type="italic">'ispı̄</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.17">Jer 10:17</reference>). Both the <hi type="italic">prosopopeia</hi> and the parallel, “thy shame shall be seen,” require that the expression “thy nakedness shall be uncovered” should not be understood literally. The shame of Babel is her shameful conduct, which is not to be exhibited in its true colours, inasmuch as a stronger one is coming upon it to rob it of its might and honour. This stronger one, apart from the instrument employed, is Jehovah: <hi type="italic">vindictam sumam, non parcam homini</hi>. Stier gives a different rendering here, namely, “I will run upon no man, i.e., so as to make him give way;” Hahn, “I will not meet with a man,” so destitute of population will Babylon be; and Ruetschi, “I will not step in as a man.” Gesenius and Rosenmüller are nearer to the mark when they suggest <hi type="italic">non pangam </hi>(<hi type="italic">paciscar</hi>)<hi type="italic">cum homine</hi>; but this would require at any rate את־אדם, even if the verb פּגע really had the meaning to strike a treaty. It means rather to strike against a person, to assault any one, then to meet or come in an opposite direction, and that not only in a hostile sense, but, as in this instance, and also in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference>, in a friendly sense as well. Hence, “I shall not receive any man, or pardon any man” (Hitzig, Ewald, etc.). According to an old method of writing the passage, there is a pause here. But <reference osisRef="Isa.47.4">Isa 47:4</reference> is still connected with what goes before. As Jehovah is speaking in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.5">Isa 47:5</reference>, but Israel in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.4">Isa 47:4</reference>, and as <reference osisRef="Isa.47.4">Isa 47:4</reference> is unsuitable to form the basis of the words of Jehovah, it must be regarded as the antiphone to <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.3">Isa 47:1-3</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa 45:15</reference>). Our Redeemer, exclaims the church in joyfully exalted self-consciousness, He is Jehovah of Hosts, the Holy One of Israel! The one name affirms that He possesses the all-conquering might; the other that He possesses the will to carry on the work of redemption - a will influenced and constrained by both love and wrath.
entries.853fd9a02545c6d7f2cfa407dd2e0dc2038de12c: <reference osisRef="Isa.47.5-Isa.47.7">Isa 47:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen13442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> In the second strophe the penal sentence of Jehovah is continued. <hi type="italic">“Sit silent, and creep into the darkness, O Chaldeans-daughter! for men no longer call thee lady of kingdoms. I was wroth with my people; I polluted mine inheritance, and gave them into thy hand: thou hast shown them no mercy; upon old men thou laidst thy yoke very heavily. And thou saidst, I shall be lady for ever; so that thou didst not take these things to heart: thou didst not consider the latter end thereof.”</hi> Babylon shall sit down in silent, brooding sorrow, and take herself away into darkness, just as those who have fallen into disgrace shrink from the eyes of men. She is looked upon as an empress (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.9">Isa 13:9</reference>; the king of Babylon called himself the king of kings, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7">Eze 26:7</reference>), who has been reduced to the condition of a slave, and durst not show herself for shame. This would happen to her, because at the time when Jehovah made use of her as His instrument for punishing His people, she went beyond the bounds of her authority, showing ho pity, and ill-treating even defenceless old men. According to Loppe, Gesenius, and Hitzig, Israel is here called <hi type="italic">zâqēn</hi>, as a decayed nation awakening sympathy; but according to the Scripture, the people of God is always young, and never decays; on the contrary, its <hi type="italic">ziqnâh</hi>, i.e., the latest period of its history (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Isa 46:4</reference>), is to be like its youth. The words are to be understood literally, like <reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">Lam 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">Lam 5:12</reference> : even upon old men, Babylon had placed the heavy yoke of prisoners and slaves. But in spite of this inhumanity, it flattered itself that it would last for ever. Hitzig adopts the reading עד גּברת, and renders it, “To all future times shall I continue, mistress to all eternity.” This may possibly be correct, but it is by no means necessary, inasmuch as it can be shown from <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.41">1Sa 20:41</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Job.14.6">Job 14:6</reference>, that (ד is used as equivalent to אשׁר עד, in the sense of “till the time that;” and <hi type="italic">gebhereth</hi>, as the feminine of <hi type="italic">gâbhēr</hi> = <hi type="italic">gebher</hi>, may be the absolute quite as well as the construct. The meaning therefore is, that the confidence of Babylon in the eternal continuance of its power was such, that “these things,” i.e., such punishments as those which were now about to fall upon it according to the prophecy, had never come into its mind; such, indeed, that it had not called to remembrance as even possible “the latter end of it,” i.e., the inevitably evil termination of its tyranny and presumption.
entries.72f38ab1078c93e0a7386726a465c9bc8eb2d468: <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8-Isa.47.11">Isa 47:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> A third strophe of this proclamation of punishment is opened here with ועתה, on the ground of the conduct censured. <hi type="italic">“And now hear this, thou voluptuous one, she who sitteth so securely, who sayeth in her heart, I am it, and none else: I shall not sit a widow, nor experience bereavement of children. And these two will come upon thee suddenly in one day: bereavement of children and widowhood; they come upon thee in fullest measure, in spite of the multitude of thy sorceries, in spite of the great abundance of thy witchcrafts. Thou trustedst in thy wickedness, saidst, No one seeth me. Thy wisdom and thy knowledge, they led thee astray; so that thou saidst in thy heart, I am it, and none else. And misfortune cometh upon thee, which thou dost not understand how to charm away: and destruction will fall upon thee, which thou canst not atone for; there will come suddenly upon thee ruin which thou suspectest not.”</hi> In the surnames given to Babylon here, a new reason is assigned for the judgment - namely, extravagance, security, and self-exaltation. עדין is an intensive from of עדן (lxx τρυφερά). The <hi type="italic">i</hi> of אפסי is regarded by Hahn as the same as we meet with in אתּי = אתּ; but this is impossible here with the first person. Rosenmüller, Ewald, Gesenius, and others, take it as <hi type="italic">chirek</hi> <hi type="italic">compaginis</hi>, and equivalent to עוד אין, which would only occur in this particular formula. Hitzig supposes it to be the suffix of the word, which is meant as a preposition in the sense of <hi type="italic">et praeter me ultra</hi> (<hi type="italic">nemo</hi>); but this <hi type="italic">nemo</hi> would be omitted, which is improbable. The more probable explanation is, that אפס signifies absolute non-existence, and when used as an adverb, “exclusively, nothing but,” e.g., קצהוּ אפס, nothing, the utmost extremity thereof, i.e., only the utmost extremity of it (Num 23:13; cf., Num 22:35). But it is mostly used with a verbal force, like אין (אין), (<hi type="italic">utique</hi>) <hi type="italic">non est</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Isa.45.14">Isa 45:14</reference>); hence אפסי, like איני, (<hi type="italic">utique</hi>) <hi type="italic">non sum</hi>. The form in which the presumption of Babylon expresses itself, viz., “I (am it), and I am absolutely nothing further,” sounds like self-deification, by the side of similar self-assertion on the part of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.5-Isa.45.6">Isa 45:5-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.21">Isa 14:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.22">Isa 14:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.46.9">Isa 46:9</reference>). Nineveh speaks in just the same way in Zep 2:15; compare Martial: “<hi type="italic">Terrarum Dea gentiumque Roma cui par est nihil et nihil secundum</hi>.” Babylon also says still further (like the Babylon of the last days in <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Rev 18:7</reference>): “I shall not sit as a widow (viz., mourning thus in solitude, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28">Lam 3:28</reference>; and secluded from the world, <reference osisRef="Gen.38.11">Gen 38:11</reference>), nor experience the loss of children” (<hi type="italic">orbitatem</hi>). She would become a widow, if she should lose the different nations, and “the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her” (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.9">Rev 18:9</reference>); for her relation to her own king cannot possibly be thought of, inasmuch as the relation in which a nation stands to its temporal king is never thought of as marriage, like that of Jehovah to Israel. She would also be a mother bereaved of her children, if war and captivity robbed her of her population. But both of these would happen to her suddenly in one day, so that she would succumb to the weight of the double sorrow. Both of them would come upon her <hi type="italic">kethummâm</hi> (<hi type="italic">secundum integritatem eorum</hi>), i.e., so that she would come to learn what the loss of men and the loss of children signified in all its extent and in all its depth, and that in spite of (בּ, with, equivalent to “notwithstanding,” as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>; not “through = on account of,” since this tone is adopted for the first time in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">Isa 47:10</reference>) the multitude of its incantations, and the very great mass (<hi type="italic">‛ŏtsmâh</hi>, an inf. noun, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Isa 30:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa 55:2</reference>, used here, not as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.29">Isa 40:29</reference>, in an intensive sense, but, like <hi type="italic">‛âtsūm</hi>, as a parallel word to <hi type="italic">rabh</hi> in a numerical sense) of its witchcrafts (<hi type="italic">chebher</hi>, binding by means of incantations, κατάδεσμος). Babylonia was the birth-place of astrology, from which sprang the twelve-fold division of the day, the horoscope and sun-dial (Herod. ii. 109); but it was also the home of magic, which pretended to bind the course of events, and even the power of the gods, and to direct them in whatever way it pleased (Diodorus, ii. 29). Thus had Babylon trusted in her wickedness (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.11">Isa 13:11</reference>), viz., in the tyranny and cunning by which she hoped to ensure perpetual duration, with the notion that she was exalted above the reach of any earthly calamity. <div eID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> She thought, “None seeth me” (<hi type="italic">non est videns me</hi>), thus suppressing the voice of conscience, and practically denying the omnipotence and omnipresence of God. ראני (with a verbal suffix, <hi type="italic">videns me</hi>, whereas ראי saere in <reference osisRef="Gen.16.3">Gen 16:3</reference> signifies <hi type="italic">videns</hi> <hi type="italic">mei</hi> = <hi type="italic">meus</hi>), also written ראני, is a pausal form in half pause for ראני (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">Isa 29:15</reference>). <hi type="italic">Tzere</hi> passes in pause both into <hi type="italic">pathach</hi> (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.42.22">Isa 42:22</reference>), and also, apart from such <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi> forms as <reference osisRef="Isa.41.16">Isa 41:16</reference>, into <hi type="italic">kametz</hi>, as in קימנוּ (<reference osisRef="Job.22.20">Job 22:20</reference>, which see). By the “wisdom and knowledge” of Babylon, which had turned her aside from the right way, we are to understand her policy, strategy, and more especially her magical arts, i.e., the mysteries of the Chaldeans, their ἐπιχώριοι φιλόσοφοι (Strabo, xxi. 1, 6). On <hi type="italic">hōvâh</hi> (used here and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.26">Eze 7:26</reference>, written <hi type="italic">havvâh</hi> elsewhere), according to its primary meaning, “yawning,” χαῖνον, then a yawning depth, χάσμα, utter destruction, see at Job 37:6. שׁאה signifies primarily a desert, or desolate place, here destruction; and hence the derivative meaning, waste noise, a dull groan. The perfect consec. of the first clause precedes its predicate רעה in the radical form בא (Ges., §147,<hi type="italic">a</hi>). With the parallelism of כּפּרהּ, it is not probable that שׁחרהּ, which rhymes with it, is a substantive, in the sense of “from which thou wilt experience no morning dawn” (i.e., after the night of calamity), as Umbreit supposes. The suffix also causes some difficulty (hence the Vulgate rendering, <hi type="italic">ortum ejus</hi>, sc. <hi type="italic">mali</hi>); and instead of תדעי, we should expect תראי. In any case, <hi type="italic">shachrâh</hi> is a verb, and Hitzig renders it, “which thou wilt not know how to unblacken;” but this privative use of <hi type="italic">shichēr</hi> as a word of colour would be without example. It would be better to translate it, “which thou wilt not know how to spy out” (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference>), but better still, “which thou wilt not know how to conjure away” (<hi type="italic">shichēr</hi> = Arab. <hi type="italic">sḥḥr</hi>, as it were <hi type="italic">incantitare</hi>, and here <hi type="italic">incantando averruncare</hi>). The last relative clause affirms what <hi type="italic">shachrâh</hi> would state, if understood according to <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Isa 26:9</reference> : destruction which thou wilt not know, i.e., which will come suddenly and unexpectedly.
entries.d898f0b211668986ec4252556fdb17edd1496fef: <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12-Isa.47.15">Isa 47:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> Then follows the concluding strophe, which, like the first, announces to the imperial city in a triumphantly sarcastic tone its inevitable fate; whereas the intermediate strophes refer rather to the sins by which this fate has been brought upon it. <hi type="italic">“Come near, then, with thine enchantments, and with the multitude of thy witchcrafts, wherein thou hast laboured from thy youth: perhaps thou canst profit, perhaps thou wilt inspire terror.
